newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT - Warner-Lambert drug pipeline.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT - Warner-Lambert drug pipeline.

text.p: Warner-Lambert Co is shedding its image as a sleepy consumer products and healthcare firm and donning the look of a hot growth company.

Two new drugs have made the difference, with investors now looking at Warner-Lambert's pharmaceutical pipeline as a main reason to buy its stock, rather than its potential as a takeover candidate, analysts said.
"In reality you're going to make your money on the pipeline no matter what happens with the takeover," said NatWest Securities analyst Jack Lamberton.

The Morris Plains, N.J.-company cleared a major hurdle toward its new status on Wednesday when a U.S. Food and Drug Administration panel voted to recommend the agency approve the potentially large-selling diabetes drug Rezulin. The FDA is not bound to panel recommendations but typically follows them.
Some pharmaceutical industry analysts estimate the diabetes drug and a cholesterol-lowering drug pending FDA review both have the potential for annual sales of $1 billion or more.
Investors took notice on Thursday, driving Warner-Lambert's stock into record territory.

Its shares were among the New York Stock Exchange's most active, up 1-1/2 to 76-7/8 in early afternoon, after hitting an all-time high of 78-3/4 earlier in the session. It rose 2-1/8 on Wednesday after the FDA advisory panel vote.

Lamberton has a 12-month price target of $100 on Warner-Lambert's stock. He estimates Rezulin could have sales of $2 billion a year in five years with the cholesterol-lowering drug atorvastatin selling $1.2 billion.
Warner-Lambert has long been better know for its consumer products, which include Rolaids antacids, Listerine mouthwash and Chiclets chewing gum.
The prescription drug side of its business was viewed as mediocre compared to other industry powerhouses, such as Merck and Co Inc, Eli Lilly and Co and Pfizer Inc.
But the new drugs have changed that, analysts said.

"Whereas (the takeover play) used to be the sole reason to own this stock, now there are multiple ways to win with this stock," said Ron Nordmann, who manages a portfolio of healthcare stocks at Deerfield Management.
Warner-Lambert had net sales of $7.0 billion in 1995, of which $2.4 billion came from its pharmaceutical business.

Because the new high-profit-margin drugs will be added to a relatively small sales base, the new drugs will have greater impact for Warner-Lambert than if they were added to the sales base of a company such as Merck, with 1995 sales of $16.7 billion, analysts said.
"It's enough to move the gross margins of the company up tremendously," said Rodman & Renshaw's James Keeney. "Therefore Warner should be one of the fastest growing drug companies."
Smith Barney analyst Christina Heuer upgraded her rating on Warner-Lambert to buy from outperform on Thursday, citing the FDA's advisory panel recommendation for Rezulin.
She put a 12-month $103 price target on the stock. Rezulin could have peak annual sales of $750 million and the cholesterol-lowering drug atorvastatin peak yearly sales of $1.25 billion, she said.
Heuer sees Rezulin being launched in the U.S. in 1997's first quarter and atorvastatin in the second half of the year.
Warner-Lambert "could become one of the hottest new drug stories of 1997," Heuer wrote in a report.
--New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1733
